articles.content: Regulator Ofgem announces that the typical annual gas and electricity bill will rise by 26% in January – described as ‘deeply worrying’ by campaigners Hannah Webster , senior economist at the think tank New Economics Foundation , also called for other measures. The price cap increase will be difficult news for households to bear, especially during the winter when our energy needs and bills are higher. The government’s current support measures don’t match the reality of rising costs and squeezed household finances. The £100 payment announced at the budget won’t cover the increase that’s coming, nor is it available to every household. According to NEF analysis, one million low-income households will miss out. Today’s price cap rise shows how exposed households remain to imported energy - the answer is to generate more at home. Biomethane, made from farms and food waste, is already flowing through our grid - enough to heat around a million homes - but NESO [National Energy System Operator] has just cut its outlook for biomethane because of policy uncertainty. Continue reading...

articles.content: Public accounts committee warns of ‘disparities in opportunities and outcomes’ depending on the type of strategic authority where people live Wes Streeting , the defence secretary, has said previous governments have engaged in a cover-up over the harm done to veterans who were involved in nuclear tests in the 1950s and 1960s. The government has launched a Hillsborough-style investigation to establish what happened. This is something campaigners have been seeking for decades. Well, we’re not going to prejudge the panel, but it’s got to lead where the facts take them. It’s got to proceed without fear or favour, and then we’ve got to act on its findings, just as we did with Hillsborough … I think the power of what Bishop James Jones [who is leading the review] will do will help us to make sure that the cover-up is exposed. articles.content: Machines are bulldozing through hard problems to assert the power of their tech bro creators, not to advance human knowledge In most walks of life, trying something 12,363,153,437,138 times and getting the same result is reason enough to assume it works every time. Not in maths, where a conjecture that holds up more than 12tn times looks very probably true but doesn’t qualify as proven. That was the status of the Riemann hypothesis, one of the most famous mathematical conundrums in existence, until last week . Then Levent Alpöge, a mathematician working at Anthropic, said he and his collaborator, Claude AI, had crossed the line from conjecture to proof. articles.content: Writer-director Beth de Araújo witnessed a brutal sexual assault as a child and has turned her experience into one of the year’s most powerful movies The film-maker Beth de Araújo likens the personal experience that inspired Josephine, her disquieting second feature, to a slow-acting poison. Early one Saturday morning when she was eight years old, Araújo and her father were playing soccer in Golden Gate Park, near their home in San Francisco, when they heard a woman scream. Her father, a former Olympic runner for Brazil, told her to stay and bolted to help; Araújo, scared and alone, ran after him, and instead found the woman in a clearing, naked from the waist down. Araújo was too young to understand what had happened, but she knew something was wrong. So, too, does an eight-year-old Josephine, played by the remarkable newcomer Mason Reeves, in the one scene crafted exactly to Araújo’s memory: Josephine, confused and restless, observes as the woman tucks her hands under her legs to keep them from shaking. She is further confused when her father, Damien, played by the aspirationally everyman actor Channing Tatum, seems extra keen to return to their soccer game afterwards, one of many echoes of Araújo’s memory in this taut drama. In real life, Araújo’s father “put on a face, put on energy and made it seem fun,” she recalled. “And I was like: ‘This is so weird. Why is my dad being so extra fun right now?’” Continue reading...

articles.author: Sali Hughes
articles.content: These fragrances are on trend right now, and smelling creamy can, it turns out, be surprisingly pleasant When the fragrance world picks a theme, it goes in hard. In the space of one month, I had close to a dozen new “lactonic” (that is, milky or creamy themed) perfumes to try. Instinctively, I wasn’t keen – I haven’t touched a glass of milk since nursery school – and so I eased myself in with DedCool’s Mocha Magic (£24 for 15ml), which adds a shot of coffee to the brand’s Xtra Milk fragrance that I love. This is immediately creamy, rich and bittersweet, like tiramisu, right down to that same dry hit of cocoa powder at the back of the throat. As in life, the coffee wears off, but the vanilla, spice and woody notes hang around for an impressively long spell. As with almost everything right now, it’s sweet, but not overbearingly so. Phlur, so beloved by gen Z, has leapt onboard the trend with Heavy Cream (from £26), available in fragrance and scented body spray. This is creamy, obviously, but also very sweet and immediately brings to mind Swizzels Drumstick lollies and the retro fizzy drink American cream soda. If this sounds like a kids’ party from hell, blame me, because it’s actually perfectly pleasant, got me heaps of compliments and got better and mellower as the hours passed. If you’re a milk with three sugars sort of a person, I think you may love it. Continue reading...

articles.content: The pair, who met in 2010, are shown preparing for the Dublin race to raise awareness of Fogarty’s epidermolysis bullosa in Rachel Fleit’s considerate documentary The personal scenes in this film from Rachel Fleit have been carefully controlled and curated, the privacy of both parties being important, for different and understandable reasons. But it is an unexpectedly intimate, emotional piece of work, a big-hearted odd-couple story, which is perhaps slightly more complex than at first appears. Emma Fogarty is a smart, garrulous woman from Abbeyleix in County Laois in the Republic of Ireland who has EB: epidermolysis bullosa, a rare condition which means that her skin is permanently, agonisingly painful and requires a daily calvary of bandaging and re-bandaging. While getting an award at the People of the year event in 2010 for her campaigning work educating the public about this illness, Emma met and struck up a friendship with Colin Farrell, a supporter and patron of the EB charity Debra Ireland . Continue reading...

articles.content: Controlled blast to proceed after multiple delays and outpouring of concern about potential health and environmental effects The US Army is set to detonate the nation’s entire stockpile of lead azide in Iowa on Wednesday morning, moving ahead after multiple delays and despite an outpouring of public concern about potential health and environmental effects. The controlled blast is planned to dispose of 9,700lb (4,400kg) of the bomb-making chemicals stored at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, a small town in south-eastern Iowa that is home to about 400 people. The explosion risks releasing plumes of toxic chemicals in a 100-mile (160km) radius, but exactly where those toxins will land has changed as the weather forecast changes. Continue reading...

articles.content: The job of Mauricio Pochettino’s successor is to fine-tune a team on the up. That requires a bureaucrat rather than a figurehead First, let’s get the Pep Exception out of the way. Or perhaps we’d better call it the Guardiola Caveat. Regardless, the point is the same. If US Soccer can get Pep Guardiola to manage the United States men’s national team, it should. Because when you have the chance to employ the most successful and influential coach of his generation, the thinker who stands upstream of essentially every major tactical current of the last two decades, you just have to do it. But let us assume that US Soccer can’t appoint Guardiola, because he is only a few months into his post-Manchester City sabbatical and still busying himself defending his body of work . Because he has given no recent indication that he wants the job, even though he spent a previous break between managerial gigs living in New York City and was probably only being supportive of his newly-appointed colleague Mauricio Pochettino when he called the project “fascinating” two years ago. Also because he has only ever signed on to coach teams stacked with Ballon d’Or contenders, posing a Phil Jackson-type, bar-room question over whether he would still be exceptional in charge of unexceptional players. Continue reading...

articles.content: Everywhere you look, there’s another unrepeatable deal at an unmissable price. What’s on offer will make you happier, smarter and sexier. Except, of course, it won’t. Let us help you ignore the ‘consumption noise’ The other morning a parcel arrived and I was momentarily mystified by its contents. Peering at what appeared to be a shiny maroon and pink cushion cover, the penny eventually dropped. It was the fancy “Sweat Bag” I had bought on impulse when it popped up on Instagram after a particularly trying day. The blurb had convinced me it was the perfect solution for storing sweaty gym gear, ensuring that everything else in my bag remained pristine. “Whether it’s a 6am class before work or squeezing in lunchtime workouts, the Sweat Bag moves with you, wherever your day takes you.” I liked the idea of being this busy, efficient human, but in reality, I generally head straight home after my workouts and collapse beside the nearest biscuit tin. I had no business spending, ahem, £39 on it. Continue reading...

articles.author: Yagnishsing Dawoor
articles.content: The Norwegian Nobel laureate’s sequel to Vaim explores what happens when a man is stripped of everything that tells him who he is Very strange things happen in Jon Fosse’s 2025 novel Vaim . A man meets a woman he secretly loved in his youth while running an errand in a nearby town. She asks him to take her away with him, to the place where they both grew up, on the boat he named after her. She wants to live with him, she tells him, even though she is married, and he has never admitted his feelings. This same man, in another section, has now died. The woman returns to her husband, and tells him he must get back with her, but he has to answer to the name she gave him when they lived together. He must also move into the home of the man she had left him for. “All was strange,” the husband admits, and decides those words should be on his tombstone. Indeed, all is – and remains – very strange to the reader: the powerlessness of these men before this woman they hardly seem to know; the randomness of the events in their lives; their spooky, dream-like surreality. But most of all: Fosse’s narrative choices that thwart easy rationalisation. Vaim Hotel is the second volume in the Nobel laureate’s loosely connected trilogy-in-progress set in the fictional Norwegian town of Vaim. Told in Fosse’s hypnotically recursive style, in a nimble translation by Damion Searls, it is ostensibly a tale of captivity that is only a touch less disorienting than its predecessor, thanks in part to the thematic correspondences it establishes. Beckettian in its relish for the absurd and the tediously mundane, this single-sentence novel opens with a man in his 50s who, for reasons he cannot quite explain, drives to Vaim, and decides to lodge at the empty Vaim Hotel, as yet unaware that he might never leave. Here, too, we have a mysterious female figure before whom male agency fails: Brita, owner of the hotel. Continue reading...

He must also move into the home of the man she had left him for. “All was strange,” the husband admits, and decides those words should be on his tombstone. Indeed, all is – and remains – very strange to the reader: the powerlessness of these men before this woman they hardly seem to know; the randomness of the events in their lives; their spooky, dream-like surreality. But most of all: Fosse’s narrative choices that thwart easy rationalisation. Vaim Hotel is the second volume in the Nobel laureate’s loosely connected trilogy-in-progress set in the fictional Norwegian town of Vaim. Told in Fosse’s hypnotically recursive style, in a nimble translation by Damion Searls, it is ostensibly a tale of captivity that is only a touch less disorienting than its predecessor, thanks in part to the thematic correspondences it establishes. Beckettian in its relish for the absurd and the tediously mundane, this single-sentence novel opens with a man in his 50s who, for reasons he cannot quite explain, drives to Vaim, and decides to lodge at the empty Vaim Hotel, as yet unaware that he might never leave. Here, too, we have a mysterious female figure before whom male agency fails: Brita, owner of the hotel. Continue reading...
articles.title: Vaim Hotel by Jon Fosse review – not your typical ghost story

articles.content: In this adaptation of the sci-fi franchise Michelle Yeoh and Hunter Schafer are on a quest to track down a group of replicants gone rogue. It’s a neon-filled world of beautiful doomsday visions Memory: the mother of the muses, and the heart of the Blade Runner franchise. Science fiction is forever asking what it means to be human and, in the future dystopia first painted by Ridley Scott’s 1982 movie, the answer is that we are what we remember: we are the experiences we preserve as a collection of short films inside our heads. In the original Blade Runner, Rachael (Sean Young) is devastated to learn that her childhood memories aren’t real, and she is therefore a robot “replicant”; in Denis Villeneuve’s sequel, Blade Runner 2049, K (Ryan Gosling) knows he’s a replicant but hopes his memories are a sign that he is something close to human. Blade Runner has always been relevant to the age of AI, in that its starting point is that enslaved robots have rebelled. But the new version, the story’s first expansion into television, is acutely topical in an era where we’re increasingly anxious about whether what we’re seeing – or reading – is the work of machines. Fifty years on from the events of the last movie, the replicants have won: “Blade runners” are now replicants hunting down disobedient humans rather than the other way around, and the capture and storage of human memories is illegal. As humanity dies, what it remembers has become valuable contraband. Continue reading...

articles.content: A new book charts the complicated relationship between the two legends, starting on a sunny afternoon in Rio in 1979 Pelé and Diego Maradona first met in April 1979, not long after the Argentinian led his country’s under-20 side to the finals of the World Youth Cup. Maradona told a journalist friend that his dream was to meet the Brazilian, and after a few weeks of aborted attempts to bring them together – mostly because Diego did not want to travel on a Monday, the one day he had free for his girlfriend Claudia – the meeting finally took place in Rio. Reporter Guillermo Blanco, who was writing about the meeting for Argentinian sports magazine El Gráfico, got the OK from Pelé’s people and was so intent on making it happen that he checked Maradona onto a flight one Sunday night without telling him. He collared the young man after Argentine Juniors played Huracán and then raced to the airport and put him on a plane with his father, his agent and a photographer. Continue reading...

articles.content: Four umpires discuss how they deal with players, why they avoid social media, how technology is changing cricket and why umpiring beats being a football referee By Wisden Cricket Monthly Last summer, sat in a quiet ground at the fag-end of a four-dayer, with a few souls still kicking around and a clutch of cameras streaming what was left of the day live on YouTube, it struck me again what a great, strange sanctuary this place is, out there on the edges of the modern world. The numbers aren’t yet earth-shattering, but how could they be, with such eccentric fare? Continue reading...

articles.author: Cath Clarke
articles.content: Tenderly drawn story combines a history of surfing with an emotional account of losing a partner to bone cancer aged 24 This gently moving and beautifully animated drama is adapted from an award-winning graphic novel by Californian illustrator AJ Dungo . His book combines a history of surfing with a memoir of love and grief; it is an account of his girlfriend Kristen Tuason, who died from bone cancer at just 24. There is something desperately sad in the film’s nostalgic mood: Dungo still in his 20s, already looking in the rearview at his youth like it’s a different universe. AJ (voiced by Will Sharpe) is a gawky teenager skateboarder who meets fun, outgoing Kirsten (Stephanie Hsu); she’s a surfer and helps AJ to overcome his fear of the ocean. Pretty soon, they’re a couple, hanging out with friends, surfing with a mixtape of sunny bright pop tunes soundtracking their teenage years. Then Kirsten is diagnosed with cancer and undergoes surgery to partially amputate her leg. When the doctors tell her she’s in remission, life goes on. Kirsten trains to be a nurse, while her brother opens a surf shop; another friend starts a craft beer business; AJ is working hard at art school. Life is ahead of them. Arguably, the film, directed by Phuong Mai Nguyen, is light on detail: characters’ facial expressions are illustrated in simple lines, the finer details of their personalities unsketched. By contrast, the ocean is rendered in spectacular depth and detail, in all its moods. There is a reverence for the sea and surfing here, and a gentle tapping into surfing’s spiritual side; a handful of gorgeous scenes in a palette of mushroom brown and grey tell snippets of its origins in Polynesia. At heart, In Waves is an idealistic, emotional film, handling its subject delicately, avoiding too much of the rawness of grief. I can imagine older kids and teenagers falling deeply in love with it. Continue reading...

articles.author: George Monbiot
articles.content: Don’t take the bait offered up by ‘conservation’ charities. Fishing is about as good for our ecosystems as tobacco is for our health Drumroll please. I am about to unveil the species of fish that’s best to eat if you want to protect the living seas. Ta-dah! It’s … I hope that clears things up. Unfortunately, over the past few years, a noisy industry has developed to tell you otherwise. You’re doing the planet a favour if you eat mackerel , sorry, cod, I mean haddock, no coley, make that pollack – oh, whoops! These choices might make you feel better about yourself. But they do nothing but harm to marine wildlife. The fish you should choose is none of the above. Cause, could I introduce you to effect? In April, the Marine Conservation Society, through its Good Fish Guide, suggested you stop eating cod and eat hake instead . Six months later, it lamented that hake is now overexploited thanks to “increased fishing pressure” , and downgraded its sustainability ratings. How on earth did that happen? Beats me. Continue reading...

articles.content: A neighbourhood that transforms into a living advent calendar, hot chocolate beneath chandeliers and 16th-century baths – Hungary’s capital is full of winter warmth Each December, my neighbourhood on the Buda side of the Danube transforms into a living advent calendar. On the edge of District XI (Újbuda), the 1930s OTI estate in Albertfalva is known for its rustic looking single-storey houses with rounded doorways and green shutters. From 1 December, my neighbours take turns decorating their windows with that day’s number and festive lights, sometimes serving chocolate, cocoa or mulled wine in their front gardens. For something grander, I’ll cross the Danube into Pest for its Christmas markets and elaborately decorated shop fronts. Last November, my friends and I sipped hot chocolate beneath the crystal chandeliers of the Művész Kávéház , a historic cafe on Andrássy út, waiting for the Christmas lights to be switched on outside, illuminating the boulevard and the Hungarian State Opera House. Continue reading...

articles.content: With my career stalled and my dreams unfulfilled, I was starting to write myself off. But my ideas about ageing were all wrong … It was the night before my wedding, in the summer of 2024, and I was a couple of months shy of 31. My bridesmaids and I were having drinks with the North American side of my family before the chaos of the big day. In the two years since I’d last seen my grandma Caroline, who lives in Texas and whom I’ve always called Memom, I’d collected a few new tattoos – and I was worried about showing them to her for the first time as her approval means a lot to me. When Memom saw me, she grabbed my tattooed arm and said: “Let me see.” For a second, I thought she was angry. But to my surprise, she loved them. “These are art!” she said. “Tell me all about them.” I talked her through the abstract fine line piece wrapping around my forearm, and why I’d opted for a filigree dagger in the middle of my upper arm, as well as the significance of the ornamental heart on the back of my right arm. Continue reading...

articles.content: Decades of data collected at WA’s Shark Bay shows level of socialising may affect longevity for Indo-Pacific bottlenose dolphins Dolphins who spend time socialising in large and consistently sized social groups tend to live longer, new research has found. articles.content: Analysis of differences in tidal height across beaches could lead to more localised tide and flood forecasts The sea might look level, but it turns out tidal height can vary by as much as a metre across the length of a single beach, new research shows. This development is important when it comes to flood predictions and when forecasting which locations are most vulnerable to storm surges. Up until now, our knowledge of tidal levels has been limited. Tide gauges tell us about a specific location, and satellite radar measurements typically average across tens of kilometres. Continue reading...

articles.author: Rich Pelley
articles.content: The Trainspotting, Slumdog Millionaire and 28 Days Later director is preparing to launch his biopic of Rupert Murdoch’s early years as a British tabloid mogul. In anticipation of its New Year release, the director will be taking your questions You name it, Danny Boyle has probably directed a movie about it. He’s done zombies in 28 Days Later, astronauts hurtling towards the sun in Sunshine, a man trapped under a boulder in 127 Hours, a world without the Beatles in Yesterday and junkies in Trainspotting. Boyle was born in Radcliffe near Manchester in 1956, and was heading towards the priesthood until, aged 14, a priest of all people talked him out of it. Instead he went into theatre, became deputy director of the Royal Court, then swerved into television, directing Inspector Morse among other things. His first film, Shallow Grave, arrived in 1994; two years later Trainspotting tore British cinema a new one. In 2009, Slumdog Millionaire won him the best director Oscar. He also masterminded the London 2012 Olympics opening ceremony, somehow squeezing industrial chimneys, NHS beds, James Bond, Mr Bean and the history of British pop into one stadium. Continue reading...

articles.author: Simon Hattenstone
articles.content: The star of Lords of Chaos, Scream 4 and Gabriel was always drawn to the dark side. Is that why he seems happier in Hollywood than his better-known brothers – and why he loved making Nocturne with Stephen Graham? Rory Culkin is enjoying the autumn afternoon in a Manhattan park. The trees are a dazzling blur of yellows, greens, oranges and reds; the background silence is so pure you can hear it. “I’m here with my baby daughter, Havoc,” he says. “Havoc Moon.” I tell him that is the spookiest name ever. “Thank you,” he says. Culkin chuckles like a revving moped, his huge blue eyes lighting up. “Yes, it’s a weird one. I think she’ll probably be the opposite. A sweet, quiet girl. She’ll play a harp or something.” He explains its origin. “I just threw out names to my partner one night when we went to dinner. She wasn’t taking to anything. I then suggested Havoc, and she really liked it. She came up with the Moon part. When we got home there was fresh graffiti on the wall across the street saying ‘Havoc’, and I was like: ‘That is a sign from the gods – we’ve got to do it.’” Continue reading...

articles.author: Flora Willson
articles.content: She has collaborated with classical giants such as Anne Sofie von Otter – and pop stars including Phoebe Bridgers. But what happened when Caroline Shaw hit ‘peak hamster wheel’? ‘Look at those!” gasps Caroline Shaw, standing next to me at an old steelworks in Germany’s industrial heartlands. Behind us are defunct concrete cooling towers and, in front, main buildings that sprawl off in a mix of brick and corrugated iron. But Shaw is looking upwards, awed by massive exhaust pipes looming overhead. This place, in the city of Bochum in western Germany, oozes post-industrial chic. These days it’s the Jahrhunderthalle , an arts venue where Shaw is performing later with the Attacca Quartet. For now the complex is shut, so we chat on a concrete bench. Intercepting Shaw, the youngest ever winner of the Pulitzer prize for music, is no mean feat: “in demand” is an understatement for this Portland-based US composer, singer, producer, violinist and viola player. Thirteen years since winning the coveted Pulitzer for Partita for 8 Voices – an exhilarating unaccompanied vocal work that mixes speech and singing, baroque dances and analogue versions of studio-mixed effects – Shaw has a CV like no other. Continue reading...

articles.author: Jonathan Liew
articles.content: Just like the ball-tampering scandal of 2018, the Brexit debate is back. The lesson here is that anything with a dodgy whiff about it will only come back Just move on. You lost, get on with it. Why rake up the past? And why, for the love of all that is holy, is Theresa May back on my television? Of all the many regrettable political figures to have surfaced over recent days, perhaps May has been most triggering of all: a bleak reminder of unhappier times. But of course she has been far from the only former prime minister lured from obscurity by the irresistible siren call of Brexit Revisited. David Cameron has been portending a “very long and painful argument”. “Divisive” and “all-consuming”, argued Rishi Sunak. Boris Johnson warned Andy Burnham – with no apparent sense of irony – that reopening the Brexit negotiations would be “wasting his premiership”. Here they come, the cast of the Tory remake of Avengers: Doomsday, presaging of rancour and paralysis from the people who brought us years of rancour and paralysis. Jonathan Liew is a sportswriter and Opinion columnist for the Guardian Continue reading...

articles.content: Victorian Liberal leader Jess Wilson’s tribute to Molly Meldrum contained heaps of the right words. But they were written by something that can’t feel I know how this will sound but when my nanna died the second thought I had, after utter devastation, was: “This is a writer’s dream.” She was 101. That is so many years old. I wrote the eulogy to end all eulogies, breaking my own heart with a bottomless well of memories, anecdotes and in-jokes. It was achingly personal and exquisitely her. The Victorian Liberal leader Jess Wilson’s team took a similar approach in this week’s tribute to the music legend Molly Meldrum , by which I mean they generated it with AI. I imagine the conversation went something like: we are 25 years old, who even was she? And then one of them plugged Molly’s name into Claude while the others went downstairs for $11 coffees. Job done. Continue reading...

articles.author: Andy Burnham
articles.content: The NDAs that enforce silence, the behaviour that exploits the age of consent. I'll address both with sweeping changes to keep women and girls safe Burnham opens door to wider NDAs ban at ‘watershed moment’ on abuse Powerful men using their fame and money to silence anyone who calls out their behaviour. Victims treated as though they’re the ones who’ve done something wrong. And a culture where abuse can hide in plain sight because people in positions of power think they can get away with it. That’s what we’ve seen in the past few weeks. This must be a watershed moment. Not just for the culture of the entertainment industry but for us as a nation. Things have improved in the past decade or so, but we are still far from being where we need to be for women and girls to feel safe and be safe. Sadly, many women and girls will find the recent stories all too close to home, whether it’s casual disrespect in the workplace, undermining “jokes”, or being told they are somehow at fault for something that has happened to them. Continue reading...

articles.content: For reasons best known to those eyeing the pound signs, Manchester City gave a debut to a special rust-coloured kit in front of a nonplussed crowd. It was of a piece with their performance for most of a familiarly frustrating night that at least concluded with a shot of energy, the home side belatedly shaking off their torpor and ending the prospect of a triumphant return to the Etihad for Kevin De Bruyne. Despite the relief sparked by a fine equaliser by Rayan Cherki, who was rewarded for an insistent but hitherto fruitless evening’s endeavours when his angled shot flashed past Vanja Milinkovic-Savic, it was hard to see this as anything but a perfect snapshot of their autumn difficulties. Nobody could pretend City were up against crack opposition in a one-paced Napoli, who are eighth in Serie A and lack the brio of old, but they simply cannot keep the door shut and could not have quibbled about departing with a defeat. articles.author: Ed Aarons at Emirates Stadium
articles.content: Arsenal’s sky-high standards are slipping. For the second time in four days, Mikel Arteta’s side found themselves a goal up at half-time and apparently coasting toward victory, only for their opponents to rouse themselves and earn a deserved draw. After Newcastle on Saturday , this time it was an impressive Borussia Dortmund who became only the second side to take points off Arsenal in their past 15 group stage games in this competition. It could have been worse had an offside flag not ruled out Jobe ­Bellingham’s goal after Max Beier equalised a thunderbolt from Viktor Gyökeres. But the much-maligned Sweden striker was guilty of a glaring miss late on as Arsenal laid siege to Dortmund’s goal, racking up 30 shots by the final whistle. The German side had to hang on for a result that gave their travelling fans a night to remember, although Arteta admitted his players must be more clinical when Real Madrid and Jude Bellingham visit north London in a fortnight. It could have been worse had an offside flag not ruled out Jobe ­Bellingham’s goal after Max Beier equalised a thunderbolt from Viktor Gyökeres. But the much-maligned Sweden striker was guilty of a glaring miss late on as Arsenal laid siege to Dortmund’s goal, racking up 30 shots by the final whistle. The German side had to hang on for a result that gave their travelling fans a night to remember, although Arteta admitted his players must be more clinical when Real Madrid and Jude Bellingham visit north London in a fortnight. articles.author: Ben Fisher at Rams Park
articles.content: This was Aston Villa’s third trip to Istanbul in the calendar year but, this time, they departed with different emotions. Unlike on the banks of the Bosphorus at Besiktas Park in May, the scene of their unforgettable Europa League triumph , or at Fenerbahce in January, they came away with a bloody nose. Galatasaray’s match-winner, Deniz Gul, finished with similar, the substitute requiring a bandage after bravely taking a boot to the face from Nicolas Jackson as the hosts rippled the net on 77 minutes. It was the game’s first effort on target, Galatasaray maintaining their commanding form on home soil to extend Villa’s winless run to six matches in all competitions. On the outside, this is a gladiatorial arena, a giant spaceship parked on Ali Sami Yen complex. But inside there is a poor pitch that began cutting up during the warm-up. John McGinn, one of four changes from Villa’s stalemate with Sunderland on Saturday, gestured towards the turf in frustration after a through ball went awry, but nobody of a Villa persuasion could blame defeat on the surface. As Unai Emery had stated, it was the same for both teams. Continue reading...

articles.author: Editorial
articles.content: Ministers have taken on board their MPs’ message about cuts. Now anxious claimants need reassurance Four million people with disabilities or long‑term health conditions in the UK claim personal independence payment (Pip). A review by Sir Stephen Timms, the social security minister, offers a blueprint for how to overhaul it . Its recommendations pose a difficult question for ministers: are they prepared to meet the needs that a more accurate assessment of the costs of disability might reveal? Sir Stephen worked as one of three co-chairs with a steering group of 12 people with a range of professional and lived experience. There is broad agreement that Pip needs to be reformed. The announcement on Tuesday that the government would accept the recommendation of a new fast track for claimants whose conditions are lifelong or unlikely to improve, and abolish unnecessary benefit reviews, signalled that ministers are ready for change. The decision, affecting one in 10 claimants in England and Wales, is welcome but long overdue. Ministers should work with the devolved administrations to ensure similar progress elsewhere in the UK. Continue reading...

articles.author: Editorial
articles.content: The PM has summarily dismissed Welsh demands for further powers similar to those enjoyed in Scotland. The approach seems at odds with his consensual style As he headed for Downing Street this summer, Andy Burnham said that he aimed to be “as collaborative and pragmatic as possible” in his dealings with the governments of Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland. His predecessor, Sir Keir Starmer, had notoriously warned ministers against being “overly deferential” in discussions with the devolved administrations. But Mr Burnham’s signature commitment to distributing more power and responsibility out of Westminster, and his consensual style, appeared to augur well for a positive reset in relations. In Wales, this early optimism has just been brutally quashed by an uncharacteristically peremptory letter from Mr Burnham to the first minister, Rhun ap Iorwerth. In it, the prime minister flatly rejected Welsh calls for the devolving of powers in relation to policing and justice, the crown estate and rail infrastructure. In the case of policing, Mr Burnham is in the curious position of denying to Mr ap Iorwerth the type of power that he enjoyed as the mayor of Greater Manchester. articles.content: Shabana Mahmood’s ‘new impartiality standard’ for police is not non-political, argues Chris Sinha . Plus a letter from Dr Peter Purton The home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, says police in uniform should not participate in LGBTQ+ pride events, saying that “at those marches, you will often have campaigners, on gender identity … and those issues are now contested … the marching alongside looks like a political act” ( Shabana Mahmood backs ban on police marching in pride events in uniform, 18 November ). She also said that it is wrong for the police not to be colour-blind in policing, as in the previous anti-racism commitment – a commitment that reflected the recognition of the history of systemic racism, and of the perceptions of the police by communities who are policed – and that the police should not engage with “activist groups and campaigners”. Instead, they should adhere to “a new impartiality standard”. Continue reading...

articles.content: The former Labour prime minister is wrong to dismiss all zero-sum thinking as misguided, writes Gavin Bailey The broad thrust of Gordon Brown’s argument is correct ( The far right is menacing Europe – but it is fragile. What the extremists and voters want isn’t the same, 22 November ). However, he is wrong to suggest that zero-sum beliefs are erroneous. Many things in life are zero-sum. If I own a house, you can’t also own it; if I burn some gas to heat it, you can’t use the same gas. If the UK makes all the cars for the European market, other countries’ carmakers won’t be making them. Yes, growth can come from collaboration and trade, but the proceeds are not infinite and take time to achieve. Continue reading...

articles.author: Guardian Staff
articles.content: The reintroduction of the birds in England and Wales spells disaster for fragile marine ecosystems, warns Tim Birkhead Your article on white-tailed sea eagle reintroduction ( Reintroduction of white-tailed eagles puts seabird colonies at risk of wipeout, say experts, 8 November ) highlighted the risk that white-tailed sea eagles are likely to pose to Britain’s seabirds. To argue, as Prof Ian Convery and Rebecca Wrigley did in their responses ( Letters, 15 November ), that the re-establishment of white-tailed sea eagles will somehow restore a lost paradise is fallacious. Where is the evidence that sea eagles will restore that balance? There is no evidence. Also, suggesting that because in the distant past sea eagles and seabirds coexisted, their reintroduction will pose no problems is naive. By failing to acknowledge that past marine ecosystems were much more robust, and seabird prey more abundant, than they are today, these two authors miss the point that it is precisely because our seabirds are currently short of food that they are so vulnerable to disturbance and predation from white-tailed sea eagles. Continue reading...

articles.author: John Crace
articles.content: Reform leader is happy to return to his anti-EU happy place, where the truth can be whatever you want it to be This feels like Nigel Farage’s happy place. It’s hardly a secret that he prefers his own company. His fellow Reform MPs are a necessary inconvenience at best. Muppets at worst. He can barely hide his misogyny for Sarah Pochin, having written her off as a pisshead. Nor does he have a much higher opinion of Richard Tice, Zia Yusuf and the others. But even Nige has worked out that when it comes to having a Potemkin alternative cabinet, he can’t realistically do everything himself. Only when it comes to Brexit, it seems, is Farage at his best as a one-man band. This is his battle. During Monday’s Commons statement, Andy Burnham said he didn’t want to keep “banging on about Europe”. But Nige most definitely does. Not least because the more he can talk about Brexit, the less people will criticise him for having no real plans for government. Most of his domestic policies collapse on contact with reality. As for foreign policy, he doesn’t have one. Unless you count having as little to do with the EU as possible. The Guardian’s year in review 2026. articles.author: Natalie Morris
articles.content: Microaggressions pile up, and then they are triggering. Amid the latest row on I’m a Celebrity, we’re obliged to explain this hurt all over again When I heard Mariella Frostrup call AJ Odudu “aggressive” over the weekend on I’m a Celebrity … Get Me Out of Here!, my heart sank with sick recognition. For her part, AJ’s mother has since said that watching her daughter experience this all-too-familiar dynamic was a “living hell”. I know many Black women tuning in will have felt a collective shudder of disgust and solidarity. Of course, there is pushback. “Our addiction to offence is tearing us apart,” wrote a Telegraph pundit on Monday . But, this language is not neutral. There is a long history of Black women having their conduct and tone disproportionately scrutinised by white people. And what happened between Odudu and Frostrup is a tale as old as time. A Black woman stands up for herself and, no matter how reasonably she presents her argument, she is accused of aggression. It is an efficient tactic to flip the focus on to the behaviour of the Black woman, and it is rooted in racist stereotypes. Natalie Morris is the author of Mixed/Other: Explorations of Multiraciality in Modern Britain Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? articles.content: The contract caterer switching to New York is a big hit to the London Stock Exchange but what is being done to discourage others from delisting? That’s gratitude, eh? Compass Group built its business, in part, on contracts to serve dinners in British schools and run catering operations in NHS hospitals. Now it plans to switch its primary stock market listing to New York in 2028. Compass is a bad one for the London market to lose. First, it is the 18th largest company in the FTSE 100 index and one of the few that is the biggest in the world in its market (contract catering, not just for the public sector but for thousands of corporate clients). articles.content: Eminent Shakespeare scholar and author who brought together the worlds of academia and the theatre In 1978 Oxford University Press made Stanley Wells, who has died aged 96, director of a Shakespeare department specially created so that he could produce a new edition of the complete works. Starting from scratch, he went back to the early printed copies, the quartos and folios, and thought through every editorial and textual decision – how to modernise the spelling and punctuation, and edit stage directions and speakers’ names, while giving the rationales for emendations. The single volume Complete Shakespeare appeared in 1986, edited by Stanley, with Gary Taylor, John Jowett and William Montgomery. It proved to be groundbreaking, startling and controversial. Continue reading...

articles.author: Benjamin Lee
articles.content: A teen girl discovers she is a witch in this mostly magic-free reminder that original animation is stuck in an unoriginal place As bleak as Disney’s overreliance on sequels might have become, it’s not quite as bleak as the crumbling state of its original output. Obviously because of the former, the latter category has become that much less populated but even when the studio has recently bothered to release something without a number in the title, it’s been hard to really see the point. With or without Pixar, films like Elio, Strange World, Raya and the Last Dragon, Luca, Elemental, Onward and Wish have all felt as uninspired as something a rival might try to desperately cobble together in an attempt to lure kids away from Disney. Three Thanksgivings ago, Wish was a particularly poor yet extremely smug example of how rubbishy things have got, a personality-free princess tale that doubled up as a 100-year anniversary victory lap. It was Disney’s worst-reviewed animated film in almost two decades and its deserved box office failure cost about $131m. Unperturbed, its co-director Fawn Veerasunthorn (along with Moana 2 director Jason Hand) is back this holiday with another rote rip-off adventure that doesn’t deserve its place in the kingdom. Continue reading...

articles.content: After the CEO was reinstated after Trump’s pressure campaign, it is abundantly clear: there are different rules for rich people There are different rules for rich people. If you or I acted the way that Jensen Huang has been accused of acting – allegedly berating and mistreating employees, sleeping with subordinates, and seeming to carry on a staggering number of extramarital affairs, including one with a woman identified by US intelligence as a likely Chinese spy who helped smuggle the company’s product to China – we probably would find ourselves out of work and out of favor for quite some time. But this is not so for Huang, the tech founder and close ally to Donald Trump who was recently ousted from Nvidia, the chip manufacturer he founded. On Monday, after a pressure campaign from Donald Trump, JD Vance and other members of the Trump administration, Huang was reinstated as CEO by the Nvidia board. articles.author: Alice Fisher
articles.content: A professor at the age of 21, Christopher Dresser was a design genius who created beautiful, futuristic homeware, from teapots to toast racks to jugs. Why is his brilliance only now being recognised? Victorian industrial designer Christopher Dresser was always a visionary. As a child, he was so artistically gifted he went to design school in 1847 when he was just 13. He became a professor at 21, dreaming up theories based on plant structure that changed the way designers worked. But it was after he quit academia that he really started to break boundaries. As a self-declared “design doctor”, he experimented with production techniques that brought beautiful, futuristic homeware into everyday houses. He was one of the first western designers to travel to Japan, helping introduce Japonisme to British life, which has had a transformative effect on furniture and decoration ever since. Continue reading...

articles.content: Sign up now! Sign up now! Sign up now? Sign up now! Sometimes, the beautiful game can make Football Daily feel old. Even Monday’s ostensibly old-school fixture between Brentford and Everton felt like the future destroying the past. The analytics-coded hosts prevailed 4-0 and James Tarkowski was dismissed by the VAR overlords for a challenge that would have been considered “firm but fair” on the muddy pitches of our youth. “I don’t think you can tackle like that in this day and age,” a misty-eyed David Moyes sighed after the game, before heading to the team bus to rewatch the Battle of Santiago . If Sunday was Gary Neville’s Sistine Chapel [ Monday’s Football Daily ], then his commentary on the Fernando Torres goal for Chelsea against Barcelona must be his David ” – Ronnie McMahon. Regarding Declan Hackett’s assertion [ Monday’s letters ] that Donald Trump will be helping his mate Mauricio Pochettino by ringing the FA to overturn Lenny Yoro’s red card, perhaps Poch should be careful what he wishes for: Trump may equally decide to get Michael Carrick reinstated, as he also has a bit of previous for that sort of thing” – Dexter O Riordan. In all the time that I have been watching football, I don’t think I have ever seen a player dismiss himself and be away down the tunnel before given a red card. Thanks James Tarkowski ” – Nigel Sanders. Brighton had only failed to win twice in the league since 5 September. A 1-1 draw with Leeds and a 2-0 defeat at Liverpool - their only opponents with double letters in their name. That bizarre hoodoo struck again at Hull on Sunday. Good good news for Seagulls fans is the only double-lettered encounters they have before hosting Hull in February are trips to Forest and Spurs. Even better news is that since that 1-1 draw with Leeds on 5 September, they have a 100% win record against sides without double letters and have not conceded a goal” – Dan Ashley (and no others). Continue reading...

articles.content: Royal Court theatre, London Ryan Calais Cameron’s ‘true(ish)’ account of a charismatic freedom fighter’s plan to take a Zambian crew to the moon never quite lifts off Ryan Calais Cameron has proved himself a playwright of stratospheric talent. His previous plays For Black Boys Who Have Considered Suicide When the Hue Gets Too Heavy and Retrograde both streaked their way into the West End. This new one is filled with mighty ambition but does not lift off in the same way. It is based on what he calls a “true(ish)” story. The figure of Edward Mukuka Nkoloso (Lucian Msamati) is taken from Zambian history. A freedom fighter for the nation’s independence in the 1960s, he set up a national academy for science and trained a group of “afronauts” in the hope of beating the US and the Soviet Union in the race to reach the moon. Nkoloso, a kind of Dead Poets Society inspiration figure here, picks 17-year-old Martha (Ama Qamata) for the mission. Continue reading...

articles.author: Madeleine Aggeler
articles.content: Before online influencers existed, the founding father published an annual wellness pamphlet. I followed his 13 virtues he found necessary for a good life Benjamin Franklin doesn’t get enough credit. Yes, he was a founding father of the United States; he invented the lightning rod and his face is printed on $100 bills. But rarely is he celebrated for his contributions to the most meaningful field of human achievement: wellness influencing. Centuries before GRWM videos and scientifically dubious podcasts were a dollar-sign-shaped glint in their creators’ eyes, Franklin was doling out life advice. Under the pseudonym Poor Richard, Franklin published an annual pamphlet and minted maxims like “Diligence is the mother of good luck” and “Fish and visitors stink after three days.” Continue reading...

But rarely is he celebrated for his contributions to the most meaningful field of human achievement: wellness influencing. Centuries before GRWM videos and scientifically dubious podcasts were a dollar-sign-shaped glint in their creators’ eyes, Franklin was doling out life advice. Under the pseudonym Poor Richard, Franklin published an annual pamphlet and minted maxims like “Diligence is the mother of good luck” and “Fish and visitors stink after three days.” Continue reading...
articles.title: Was Benjamin Franklin the original wellness bro? I lived like him for a day to find out

articles.author: Geoffrey Robertson
articles.content: Proving the ‘crime of crimes’ against an individual is notoriously difficult, but the ICJ has set a precedent for states to be found liable. Israel could be next For the first time ever, a state has been found guilty of genocide – that “crime of crimes” – and has been ordered to compensate victims and to prosecute and punish the perpetrators. This judgment came from the international court of justice (ICJ), which has convicted Myanmar of killing and expelling many thousands of Rohingyas in Rakhine state in 2017 . The court did not change the definition of the crime, settled by the genocide convention in 1948 as requiring proof of an intention to destroy, in whole or part, a racial or religious group as such. But it made the prospect of proving this against a nation a good deal easier than against an individual. It set a precedent for its next case concerning state liability, namely the case brought by South Africa against Israel. Geoffrey Robertson KC was a UN appeal judge and is author of World of War Crimes – Eyeless in Gaza and Beyond Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? articles.author: Charlotte Jansen
articles.content: The Photographers’ Gallery, London Sanlé Sory is known for his black and white images taken during independence in Burkina Faso – but his colour portraits bring humour, insouciance and joy Despite his wide renown, there have been hardly any major exhibitions of Sanlé Sory’s work. His last UK show was in 2019, concentrating on the black-and-white images the Burkinabé photographer made in the first two decades after opening his own studio, Volta Photo, in Bobo-Dioulasso in 1960 – a period that coincided with the first two decades of independence in Burkina Faso. This new Photographer’s Gallery show shifts the focus to the 1980s and 1990s, when Sory began working in colour. It’s easy to see why, even with few exhibitions, Sory has made such an impression on audiences. There are the familiar west African studio photography tropes westerners love, where sound, image, fashion and pose collide. The props are popping, the style is irrepressible, the energy is irresistible. I wonder if Sory’s speed and instinct came from the time he spent early in his career racing on his motorbike to photograph car accidents for newspapers and the police. These portraits are the opposite of a car crash, they’re remedially joyful, wilfully alive – but they share that feeling of being inside the moment, at the edge of something. Continue reading...

articles.author: Anna Berrill
articles.content: Festive drinks are all about capturing the warmth and theatre of the season, so lean into wintry flavours such as orange and cloves, and add a bit of drama by bringing out the blowtorch What are the best cocktails to make for a Christmas party? Dan, by email We’re all in favour of getting the party season started early, Dan, so now is as good a time as any to get your drinks cupboard in order. “Ultimately, Christmas cocktails are all about bringing a little warmth, nostalgia and theatre, so don’t be afraid to have fun with seasonal flavours,” says Josie Pink, author of River Cottage: Cocktails and Botanicals . The smell of orange, be it fresh or dried, is never too far away at this time of year, and one reason Pink suggests having a batch of orange liquor on hand, not least “to rustle up a margarita or two”. Ditto dried citrus wheels: “They’re a must,” she says. “Not only are they gorgeous for adorning cocktails, but any misshapes can be turned into marmalade dust, and any spares into home decorations.” Pink also advises getting some syrups in your arsenal – “I’d opt for a batch of trusty vanilla syrup” – plus a chai number “for those fragrant, warming spice flavours that we all associate with the festive season”. If there’s a gang coming over, you’ll likely find Pink ladling hot mulled apple juice laced with citrussy gin into mugs, or making pitchers of rum punch: “Either would warm the cockles.” Alternatively, consider a “slightly lighter” mulled white wine: “Gently warm your favourite white wine with spices such as star anise, cinnamon, ginger and cloves, sweeten with syrup and citrus, then spike with apple cider brandy.” Got a culinary dilemma? Email feast@theguardian.com Continue reading...

If there’s a gang coming over, you’ll likely find Pink ladling hot mulled apple juice laced with citrussy gin into mugs, or making pitchers of rum punch: “Either would warm the cockles.” Alternatively, consider a “slightly lighter” mulled white wine: “Gently warm your favourite white wine with spices such as star anise, cinnamon, ginger and cloves, sweeten with syrup and citrus, then spike with apple cider brandy.” Got a culinary dilemma? Email feast@theguardian.com Continue reading...
articles.title: The secret to the perfect Christmas party cocktail

articles.author: Jonathan Jones
articles.content: London Museum Smithfield Why has the revamped museum divided its exhibits into nonsensical themes and shunted all the fascinating stuff downstairs? The results are baffling, unengaging and soulless ‘ An astonishing sight’: Oliver Wainwright reviews the building’s architecture The Museum of London at the Barbican was the capital’s local museum, a crowded and quirky presentation of its history from the Dagenham idol to Vauxhall Pleasure Gardens . But apparently the location deterred casual visitors, and maybe it just wasn’t grand enough to reflect London’s self-conscious significance. For not since ancient Rome has a capital dominated its nation’s history and culture like London. So now we get the rebranded and reimagined London Museum Smithfield. History surrounds you in this neighbourhood: Black Death burials by the Charterhouse, the Knights of St John, the Smithfield martyrs, William Wallace’s execution site. So goodbye scruffy brutalist Slough House location, hello deep history. Except when you enter the new museum, all that history, all those layers going back to the Romans and earlier, have been brushed away. If you want an illustration that bigger is not better, this is it. When Sharon Ament, the director, asked me if I liked it, I couldn’t find the words. I was heartbroken, speechless, unlike the museum’s management who have their own way with language. Displays have nonsensical themes: “London as Ritual”, “London as Stage”, “London as Sunrise”. One wall text begins: “London is a city of people.” Read that twice. What is this? Cunk on London? Continue reading...

articles.author: Niki Segnit
articles.content: Plus five fantastic recipes, from seared tuna and potato to spicy butternut and lentil, to show how it’s done Approach a winter salad as you would your winter wardrobe – with clever layering. With the greatest respect to Coco Chanel, and her famous rule about taking one item off when you think you’re done, in this instance I favour assembling a salad and then adding an ingredient. Unlike in baking, where departing from a recipe can have its risks, improvisation rewards the salad maker. Still, if you’re planning a winter salad, especially if it’s a main meal, you might want to use a checklist to avoid some common pitfalls. The most egregious of these is cosy dullness. It’s all too easy to throw together some fresh winter produce and end up with a dish that’s more like a cold risotto or yesterday’s traybake. This often comes down to the combination of roasted root vegetables and “interesting” grains. What makes a salad a salad is its invigorating qualities, but root veg and cereals are sweet, with earthy, nutty flavours and soft textures; the pairing might be a modern classic but it’s about as invigorating as a warm bath. Not that you should avoid the combination; you just want to balance it with ingredients that offset its soporific qualities. It’s a good stress test for our guidelines, in fact: if you can turn a root-and-grain combination into a bright and balanced salad, you’re on to a winner. Continue reading...

articles.author: Alyssa Mercante
articles.content: Given that this is the first Grand Theft Auto in 30 years with a female protagonist, you might have expected to hear from female critics. But you would have expected mostly in vain Grand Theft Auto VI is now the biggest video game launch of all time, and is likely to become the biggest video game of all time. It’s a once-in-a-lifetime event, a phenomenon that will shape games as a medium and pop culture at large for years to come, set against the backdrop of its developers fighting for their rights at studio Rockstar Games . It has snatched sales and streaming records and become the best-reviewed game ever (pulling ahead of 1998’s The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time). It’s also the first GTA game with a female protagonist, who also happens to be a woman of colour. Yet very few women (and seemingly no women of colour) played and reviewed it before release. When GTA VI’s review embargo lifted on 18 November, the gender imbalance was immediately obvious. Out of 156 reviewers, only six appeared to be women. As journalist Lex Luddy noted in a BlueSky post , that is 3.8%. Continue reading...

articles.author: Aaron Timms
articles.content: For big stars, endorsing companies like Kalshi and Polymarket is just another day in the beautiful business of being – and staying – rich When Giannis Antetokounmpo announced he was taking an investment stake in prediction market Kalshi in February, the claim he made to accompany the announcement – “We all on Kalshi now” – sounded as absurd as the howls of outrage from sports lovers seemed universal. Nine months later, Kalshi’s grip on American fans appears murderously tight: notional monthly trading volume on the platform, the majority of which is taken up by wagers on sports, increased to nearly $100bn in October from $40bn in August, as the company gears up for yet another funding round at a rumored valuation of $65bn ahead of a potential IPO. Rival prediction market Polymarket, which relaunched in the US late last year after regulators shut it down in 2022, has seen similar growth over recent months. However righteous the disgust from fans on social media at the deepening incursion of these odious platforms into professional sport may be, their popularity seems only to grow. More perplexing is the widening circle of athletes like Giannis who’ve thrown off whatever shame might once have come from association with these businesses and given them their full-throated support. The line between role model and shill in professional sports is now essentially non-existent. Pete Sampras, a man so private in retirement it can often seem like his entire tennis career was a collective hallucination, released an ad for Kalshi during this year’s US Open after two decades largely out of the public eye. José Mourinho trousered a brick of Kalshi cash this summer in exchange for a gambling promo during the World Cup. The prediction market machine now sponsors Jalen Brunson and Josh Hart’s Roommates Show, on which the recently crowned pair of NBA champions begin every episode dutifully informing us that their amazingly dreary podcast is “presented by Polymarket, the top prediction market”. LeBron James will make more from his recently announced partnership with Polymarket – $15m a year – than he will from playing for the Philadelphia 76ers. Somehow we’ve arrived at the point where it’s bigger news if a professional athlete takes a firm stand against the prediction markets, as Victor Wembanyama recently did , rather than pockets the cash to endorse them. Continue reading...

articles.content: Pick wisely, and your fake fir could be reused for decades of Decembers. From pre-lit to frosted to space-saving, here are our festive favourites • The best beauty Advent calendars • The best Christmas baubles In the 70s and 80s Essex of my youth, no one had a real Christmas tree unless they lived in the country, or perhaps Loughton. Our family’s skinny artificial tree is now 55 years old and comes out every year at my sister’s. It’s shed a few plastic “needles” down the years, but it’s still standing proud – which is more than you can say for a real Christmas tree bought in 1971, or even 2025. Therein lies the surprising environmental efficiency of artificial Christmas trees. The Carbon Trust says using a fake tree over seven to 20 years (depending on its weight and materials) can create fewer emissions than buying a new, commercially grown tree every year. The key is to buy an artificial tree you’ll love enough to roll out for decades. Continue reading...

articles.author: Leslie Felperin
articles.content: A livestock farmer with a sad secret in her past rallies to keep military training out of her breathtaking mountain home in Montenegro An award-winner in Sundance, where it premiered earlier this year, this slow-burn documentary follows a middle-aged Montenegrin livestock farmer called Gara and her 13-year-old daughter Nada. The two of them eke out a hardscrabble living on Sinjajevina, a breathtaking mountain plateau on which Montenegro’s government would like to conduct training exercises for its own army as well as Nato’s. This goes down about as well as a wolf in the sheep pen with flinty Gara, who rallies her neighbours as well as the local media to fight the proposal. She displays a savviness that’s somewhat surprising, even if her fortitude and strength of conviction seem completely in character. However, that fight against the state is just one element of a film that, through long, languid takes, reveals the women’s stately pastoral existence, one taken up above all with care for their menagerie of animals (cows, sheep, goats, cats and dogs) and each other. Co-directors Petar Glomazić and Biljana Tutorov gradually reveal the family setup isn’t exactly what it appears at first. Although Gara calls Nada her daughter, the young girl is actually her niece; Gara adopted her after her sister, Nada’s mum, was killed by a violent husband. Gara’s profound grief and loss haunt her every day, felt most painfully, perhaps, when an animal dies on the heath, reminding them of the fragility of life. Continue reading...

articles.content: Winger has not played for the USMNT since the World Cup and believes good club form is his route back into the squad This was the USMNT’s summer. By extension, it was also that of the 26 players selected by Mauricio Pochettino to represent the nation at a home World Cup. It didn’t live up to expectations for all of them, and certainly not for Timothy Weah. “Obviously this summer wasn’t the best for me,” he says. Weah was one of eight players in the squad to have started all four of the US’s matches in Qatar in 2022. He remained a regular heading into this tournament but would ultimately start only one game in a campaign that came to an end at the hands of Belgium in the last 16 . “In every career you have moments where you’re a bit down, and you’re a bit in your head about things. I think the World Cup was definitely that for me,” Weah says. “On a personal level, I had to take a back seat and figure out where my place was in the squad.” Continue reading...

articles.author: Jesse Hassenger
articles.content: With the British actor securing the role of James Bond, speculation has now begun over who should join him in Denis Villeneuve’s much-anticipated caper After years of speculation, Robert Pattinson has been officially cast as James Bond for a new Amazon-produced film directed by Denis Villeneuve. There’s no release date for the project yet, though fall 2028 seems a likely target, given the release dates of all of the Pierce Brosnan and Daniel Craig installments. This leaves plenty of time left on the clock for more speculation – namely, about who will be cast as the so-called Bond Girls for this rebooted installment. Past Bonds have usually been recognizable from earlier work, but none of them had yet reached Pattinson’s level of fame before actually playing Bond. Given that, in addition to sterling indie work for directors like David Cronenberg, Claire Denis and Lance Oppenheim, Pattinson has also been in Twilight, Batman and Christopher Nolan movies, he’s arguably already as famous as Brosnan and Craig were at their 007 peak. It must be this shift in the casting status quo that has inspired some predictions or hopes for a quantity as known as, say, Sydney Sweeney to play a Bond girl. Continue reading...

articles.author: Peter Bradshaw
articles.content: Yoon Ga-eun’s film tracks the uneasy fallout after a teenage schoolgirl makes a deeply shocking announcement to her class Korean film-maker Yoon Ga-eun creates a strange world of bewilderment, sadness and pain – but not much of love – in this involving and mysterious family drama. It seems always to be gesturing at an indefinable sense of loss, a poignant keynote struck by the recurring soundtrack piano arrangement of Bach’s Sheep May Safely Graze. Seo Su-bin gives an excellent performance as Joo-in, a high schooler possessed of a cheeky, madcap sense of fun, like her wacky, magic-obsessed kid brother Hae-in (Lee Jae-hee). She is keen on taekwondo and often shown (in borderline-uncomfortable closeup) kissing boyfriends that she will later dump. But when classmate Su-ho (Kim Jeong-sik) asks her to sign a petition objecting to the release and local rehousing of a convicted child rapist, Joo-in refuses, on the ostensible grounds that the petition talks about the permanent damage done to rape victims. Joo-in astonishes and upsets the class by announcing at the top of her voice that she herself is a rape victim, and she has not been permanently damaged – and then says it was just a joke. Continue reading...

articles.content: A disturbing account of the way Russia’s elites have reduced themselves to craven courtiers When Vladimir Putin launched his full-scale invasion of Ukraine four and a half years ago, it was a shock, but it wasn’t a surprise. The US and the UK had been publicly warning their allies for weeks about what Russia was planning, as well as threatening the Russians with a wave of sanctions unprecedented against a major power. Putin’s foreign policy had long relied on confusion and untruth. By saying that they knew exactly what he was up to, Britain and America were hoping first to deny him his usual ambiguity, and second to pressure the men around him into making him stop, since war would deprive them of the stolen assets they’d stashed in London’s most exclusive neighbourhoods. Continue reading...

articles.author: Fergal Kinney
articles.content: Once the historic centre of the textile industry, the north is now home to a host of a provenance-driven labels. But is there a specific northern menswear look? And what does it all mean for the mad-fer-it stereotypes? In 2026, clothing has proved more important to Andy Burnham’s political identity than that of any British prime minister since Margaret Thatcher. He is a loyal Clarks and Adidas wearer, whose Howick worker’s jacket hangs in Manchester’s People’s History Museum. His ousting of Keir Starmer – launched shortly before being photographed jogging in a replica Everton shirt – has been memorialised as the “casual coup”. In one telling, the reason for this is simple: he’s a man from the north. That Burnham is the first born-and-bred northern male PM since Harold Wilson last swished his Gannex raincoat out of Downing Street goes some way to explaining his higher interest in clothing. It’s not necessarily that all men in the south care less about clothing, or that all men in the north do – but that many men from the north express it in such a distinctive, even unified, way. Continue reading...

articles.author: Angela Giuffrida
articles.content: There is plenty of sunshine, the tourists have thinned out – and no one does a traditional Christmas like the Romans There was a time when, during a Rome winter, I would crave the warmer months. Not any more. The combination of intense heat and overtourism has made summer poco piacevole , as Italians would say – not very pleasant. So come mid-September, when the temperature drops and the crowds thin out, our mood lifts as we reclaim the city and slip back into familiar routines. In winter, the temperature is mostly mild and there is still plenty of sunshine (we do tend to grumble if the rain and grey skies persist for a few days). Rome is best seen on foot, and my favourite time to walk it is on a Sunday. Until earlier this year, I lived in Esquilino, a vibrant neighbourhood close to Termini train station. I’d begin with coffee at Gatsby Cafe by Piazza Vittorio before walking along Via Merulana – a tree-lined street similar to a Parisian boulevard – and then through the Colle Oppio park, past the Colosseum and towards Circo Massimo . Continue reading...

articles.author: Rich Pelley
articles.content: When a neighbour installed a braying bird on the roof of our block of flats, the noise was relentless from sunrise till sunset. It became the sinister soundtrack to my life You can’t choose your family or your colleagues. And you definitely can’t choose your neighbours: the people with whom you involuntarily share a postcode and the ritual of swapping misdelivered Amazon parcels. For the most part, the neighbours in my block of flats are reassuringly neighbourly. During lockdown, I became unofficial IT support for one trying to home-school her son. I spent years emailing a PR man about Guardian celebrity interviews without realising he lived two doors away. And one of my neighbours (and now my hero) used to be in the 80s punk band Splodgenessabounds, who sang Two Pints of Lager and a Packet of Crisps Please. The other half I couldn’t pick out of a police lineup, although I certainly know their habits, from the phantom non-recycler who bungs all their plastic bottles and newspapers in the normal black bin, to the mystery resident who happily leaves the security gate open. But the one that is lodged most firmly in my memory is the neighbour who, last year, kept a pet cockerel on the roof. At least, I assume it was a pet. I can’t think of any other reason that doesn’t sound considerably more sinister. Continue reading...

articles.author: Beejay Silcox
articles.content: The afterlife of a Yorkshire village girl who becomes a gothic literary icon is explored across three centuries, in a thrilling paean to the power of books I had a plan. I was going to nibble away at this great wedge of a book, a morsel a night, like a little reading mouse. But then the story swallowed me whole. I read Dutch author Anjet Daanje’s The Song of Stork and Dromedary over three feverish nights, and spent the days in between longing for the dark. This 720-page novel should come with a warning label: may cause severe infatuation. We begin in the fictional Yorkshire village of Bridge Fowling with Susan Knowles-Chester, a woman who attends to the dead. The year is 1847, and Susan knows the old ways, the threshold rituals: how to arrange a corpse so it doesn’t gape and gawp at the living. “The villagers have a horror of her work, for wherever she goes, she leaves grief like driftwood in her wake, yet when the time comes, many ask for her help, it is an open secret.” Continue reading...

articles.content: Creedy Valley, Devon: Three oaks in a row – one is green, one is bronze and the other is shedding its golden leaves like a shaken snow globe Leaves fall from the oak on the brow of the hill in a flurry. There is only a slight wind, yet it is as though a snow globe has been shaken – so many leaves are animated. The process seems to take a long time. Mesmerised, I follow as they glitter to the ground. There are oaks on either side of this one. To the right, despite its close proximity, the tree has not felt the same call to let its leaves go. Instead, it holds them close – a burnished bronze, brighter even than its neighbour’s gold. To the left, a greener tree stands on the end of the line. Continue reading...

articles.content: The character comedian AKA Lee Nelson handed May a P45 and threw golf balls at Donald Trump. He explains why the pranking’s now on ice – and which funny footballers inspired him How did you get into comedy? I was booted out of every class for making jokes and then I discovered, at medical school, there is such a thing as a career in comedy. I was encouraged by being able to entertain the patients and went straight from that into comedy. Who did you admire when you were starting out? It was always the character comedians: Sacha Baron Cohen, Ricky Gervais, Steve Coogan. On the circuit Al Murray was doing the Pub Landlord. I admired anyone doing characters who could be dropped into multiple situations. As I started doing character comedy myself, I was inspired by people who might not have known how funny they were, such as a big batch of Premier League footballers from Beckham to Gerrard to Rooney. Simon Brodkin: Unleashed is at the Apollo, London , on 13 December and 11 March and on tour in the UK until 26 May Continue reading...

articles.content: The Summer I Turned Pretty’s Christopher Briney and 1923’s Michelle Randolph try their best, but this chaotic cross-country journey is not worth taking Credit where credit is due: it takes some nerve for Amazon to open its latest holiday romcom, Clashing Through the Snow, with characters bemoaning the enervated state of the book industry. Publishing isn’t the cultural epicenter it once was, reports boutique press head Jeremy (PJ Byrne) before announcing some impending new year’s layoffs. Alas, things have changed – “if Faulkner were alive today, he’d be making ASMR videos with Mr Beast” (or, perhaps, competing on Prime Video’s Beast Games?) Self-awareness can be key to the ludicrous joys of a Christmas romcom confection, though Clashing Through the Snow, starring 1923’s Michelle Randolph and homegrown Amazon star Christopher Briney (The Summer I Turned Pretty), tests one’s patience for beating you to the branded punchline. Briney’s Ryan, a numbers-driven, macro-counting kind of book editor, pitches a “financial trends with benefits” romance that could be “Rebecca Yarros big”. Soulmates, says Randolph’s rival workhorse editor Hannah, are as mythical as “ethical billionaires and pain-free bikini waxes”. Due to said budget cuts, both have a week to land “a book so big it makes Harry Potter look like a Buzzfeed listicle” for only one to keep their job. What are two LA workaholics going to do on Christmas but take meetings in New York? Continue reading...

articles.author: Nadia Khomami
articles.content: The evidence seems overwhelming, but artists and writers have borrowed from each other for hundreds of years. The line between homage and theft is a thin one “Immature poets imitate; mature poets steal,” the poet TS Eliot wrote a century ago. No work of art, he argued, exists in a vacuum. Great writers draw on what came before them, transforming their influences into something entirely their own. Eliot’s words came to mind when I read the revelations about the queen of the country house bonkbuster Jilly Cooper, who has been accused of “extensive and deliberate” plagiarism in her 1978 book Prudence. At least 35 passages appear to have been lifted from The Serial, a satirical novel by American writer Cyra McFadden, alongside remarkable similarities to sections of Josephine Tey’s 1948 novel The Franchise Affair. McFadden’s daughter is threatening legal action, describing the treatment of her mother’s work as “unconscionable”. Nadia Khomami is arts and culture correspondent at the Guardian Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to submit a response of up to 300 words by email to be considered for publication in our letters section, please click here . Continue reading...

articles.content: Wigmore Hall, London Centred around the world premiere of jazz bassist Misha Mullov-Abbado’s almost-concerto, the tight ensemble took a tour of classical fusion and tango fisticuffs In this eclectic programme of mostly 21st-century music, the United Strings of Europe found the intersection in a Venn diagram of chamber music, string orchestra and jazz. At its centre, receiving its world premiere, was The Travelling Violin by the jazz bassist and composer Misha Mullov-Abbado . In four movements, it’s an almost-concerto on an intimate scale. The solo violin, deftly played here by Tamsin Waley-Cohen, has the narrating role, but the writing for the nine supporting string instruments is so intricately woven that it feels like an ensemble piece. It almost seemed strange for Waley-Cohen to give a solo encore at the end, mesmerising though her playing of Nicola Matteis Jr’s A minor Fantasia was. Mullov-Abbado’s piece has a role for jazz bass, which he played himself, and for percussion, from soft-edged shimmering to driving, grooving drums, played by Fred Thomas; the jazz sensibility of both of these leaches into the rest. Led by the violinist Julian Azkoul, the ensemble was tight, churning over the tricksy rhythmic figures of the faster movements and radiating warmth in the third, which sounded like Cole Porter reflected in a slightly warped mirror. Mullov-Abbado’s violin writing is as gratifying as you’d hope for from the son of Viktoria Mullova , and his jazz-classical fusion hits an unusually effective sweet spot. Continue reading...
