articles.author: Xan Brooks
articles.content: With Musk, NAZA and You Can See Everything finding large audiences, non-fiction cinema is poised to break through. But there are plenty more gripping stories waiting for their turn in the spotlight There comes a time in the life of every film enthusiast when they must set aside foolish fictions and face up to some hard truths. Specifically, that time arrives each November in the form of the International Documentary Film Festival Amsterdam (IDFA for short), with its tales of crisis and strife, angry resistance and everyday human kindness. The world’s largest documentary festival plays out in the city’s twinkling downtown district, quite near the torture museum, and provides a sharp corrective to the confected dramas and A-list pageantry of Cannes, Toronto and Venice. The forecast is bracing, stormy, and occasionally chilling. Hours of darkness; no stars. We might not wish to live in the world IDFA shows us, but unfortunately we do, and so it pays to stay informed, be engaged. This year’s lineup of 250-plus documentaries steers us around the geopolitical hot spots, from tales of forced displacement in the West Bank to the rolling hell of Gaza; from a jungle-based guerrilla army in Myanmar (in White Tiger Column, the event’s opening night film) through to the traumatised children of the Vietnamese boat people (Carol Nguyen’s superb Still Night, Burning House). Some of these films could have been torn from the headlines. Others, like Raluca Lupascu’s gripping kitchen-sink tragedy A Modern Roma Fairytale, contain stories previously tucked away out of sight, just waiting to be told. Continue reading...

articles.content: The death and pain of female characters has always been a bedrock of opera. Kaija Saariaho and today’s female composers are challenging this narrative, and thereby connecting with today’s world In 1992, the Finnish composer Kaija Saariaho saw a Salzburg festival production of Messiaen’s Saint François d’Assise. A series of meditative theological tableaux in which naturalism and plot is secondary to the revelation of deeper spiritual truths, it is now hailed as a masterpiece although it divided critics on its Paris premiere in 1983. Saariaho, one of the painfully few female composers in opera’s 400-year history, recalled thinking: “If that is an opera, then I can write one”. And she did, to notable international acclaim. Her first opera L’Amour de loin (Love from Afar), a tale of medieval courtly love with a libretto by war correspondent and writer Amin Maalouf was premiered, appropriately, at 2000’s Salzburg festival and came to the UK when English National Opera staged it in 2009 . Continue reading...

articles.content: If you’re a cyberpunk who loves ennui and watching actors you can’t see speak words you can’t hear, get stuck in! The rest of us will just be baffled and bored Why is James Bond not a TV series by now? Harry Potter, Lord of the Rings, Alien, Star Wars – all given the TV treatment. Franchise-mining is fantastic business, maximising attention share in order to sell adverts. So why not Bond, which is co-owned by Amazon? Maybe watching a punchy sex addict every week, saying his name with weirdly administrative syntax, might just be … too much? I entertained these thoughts while struggling to get through another series expansion: Blade Runner 2099 (Prime Video, from Wednesday). I’m a fan of the films. Before the original, cinema had imagined the future as serene and orderly. Blade Runner introduced many of us to novelist Philip K Dick’s vision, in which tech has colonised every aspect of life, but inequality has got worse. Surveillance, artificial beings and unchecked corporate power hollow out whatever remains of society. (The fact the new series is on Amazon is the closest it gets to making a joke.) Continue reading...

articles.content: Royal & Derngate, Northampton The Black Books star gets off to a promising start as he contemplates ‘the burning ball of what you don’t understand’ but his search for levity leads to half-baked ditties Is Dylan Moran joking when he opens his show by telling Northampton’s audience “I didn’t write anything, or prepare”? By the end, you wouldn’t bet on it. Bleary directionlessness may be par for the course for the Irish comic, whose work has always combined poetic-philosophical dazzle with a certain wooziness. But after a promising start tonight, his new touring show, Looking for Trouble, conspicuously loses its way, as Moran frets about forgetting a significant chunk of material, before abandoning his encore and leaving a bewildered audience in his wake. That’s a shame, because there are shards of trademark brilliance in the opening 20 minutes, which see the 55-year-old address himself, albeit obliquely, to the mysteries of being human in 2026, AKA “the burning ball of what you don’t understand” From Trump to AI, Moran surveys it all in wide angle not closeup, as symptoms of our confusion, atavism and fear of expulsion from the tribe. The quality of his thinking in this section, while cheerfully offering himself up as Exhibit A in this prosecution of humanity’s perplexity, is arresting. And there are zingers, too, including a word-picture of the genitals that, once heard, may never be forgotten. Continue reading...

articles.content: From Heated Rivalry to Harry Potter, popular series are inspiring fan fiction read by thousands online. Now the authors of those online works are getting publishing deals of their own Shortly after this year’s London book fair , rumours began to circulate of a seven-figure book deal for the author of the wildly popular work of Harry Potter fan fiction All the Young Dudes. First published between 2017 and 2018 by user MsKingBean89 on the online platform Archive of Our Own, All the Young Dudes is arguably the most-read work of fan fiction of all time. Now its author will write a trilogy under the pen name BN King, with the first novel, Wolfboy, due to be published in autumn 2027. This is by no means the first example of fan fiction crossing over into mainstream publishing: the bestselling debut of 2025, Alchemised, also started off as fan fiction based on the Harry Potter series, with some inspiration from The Handmaid’s Tale too. And nearly 15 years earlier, EL James published Fifty Shades of Grey, which began life as Twilight fan fiction before proceeding, in its new guise, to sell millions of copies worldwide. Continue reading...

articles.content: As he invests in 60,0000 sq ft of midwest real estate, the celebrated artist explains bringing ‘independent thinking’ back to fine china “The worth of hand-painted china depends mainly upon the hand ,” reads an advertisement dating from 1910 and displayed just inside the entrance of the Pickard China factory, a sprawling, 60,000 sq ft brick building just outside Chicago. “Most of the large staff of artists at the Pickard studios have been trained in the great art centers of Europe, and each piece of Pickard is painted from start to finish by the same master craftsman.” Those statements are a distant echo from another age. These days, Pickard – the last operational porcelain fine china factory in the US – is in a shocking state of disrepair, its 12 remaining employees struggling to fulfill longstanding orders for the White House (Pickard began producing official White House china in 2008 when the company was commissioned by Laura Bush), Williams Sonoma, US embassies, private golf clubs and anxious brides-to-be. Continue reading...

articles.content: The latest in our series of writers picking their most rewatched comfort films is an ode to Eddie Murphy’s beloved culture-clash comedy “Good morning, my neighbors!” A young Eddie Murphy shouts from the balcony of a shady apartment building. In the bustling Queens neighborhood, he sticks out like a sore thumb with his foreign accent, tailored blazing jacket and red tie. “Hey, fuck you!” A voice yells from below and Murphy repeats the phrase, believing that it’s a greeting rather than an insult. It’s one of the standout scenes from the film Coming to America, because it’s so absurd but effective in that there is a cultural clash going on here. In Coming to America, Prince Akeem, played by Eddie Murphy, is the sole heir to the throne of Zamunda, a fictitious African country. Instead of having an arranged marriage, Prince Akeem exercises his autonomy and intends to find his own bride somewhere far away from the continent, much to his parents’ chagrin. With the coin-flip and a roll of the personal globe, Akeem and his sidekick Semmi go to America but more specifically Queens because where else would be more fitting to find his bride? While trying to assimilate to the fast pace of New York living, he pursues Lisa, the heiress to a different kind of throne – that of a fast-food business called McDowell’s. The problem is, she’s already engaged to another. Akeem hides his identity as a royal prince and works at her father’s fast-food restaurant to get closer to her. Will Akeem and Lisa fall in love as he cosplays being working class. Will Lisa leave her rich but arrogant fiance? Will their families accept their Lisa and Akeem if they do decide to marry? Spoiler alert: there’s a happy ending. The plot progression is simple but the character development is full of heart and candor. Continue reading...

articles.content: The idea that we access a fraction of our cognitive potential goes back decades, but does medical science agree? This idea really bugs Dr Mary Spiller , senior lecturer in the University of East London’s Department of Psychology and Human Development, who’s shocked by how prevalent it remains, despite being untrue. Spiller says the myth’s origins can partly be traced to the work of William James, one of the founders of modern psychology, working in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. He wrote: “We are making use of only a small part of our possible mental and physical resources.” Continue reading...

articles.author: Paul Sullivan
articles.content: The cold is legendary, but there’s hot chocolate and Glühwein to warm you up, plus crowd-free museums and galleries and cosy candlelit pubs One of the first things Berliners warned me about when I moved here in 2008 was the winters. They talked in hushed, conspiratorial tones about the harsh winds that blew in from the Russian steppes, temperatures of minus 15C and the horrors of frozen bike locks. Having survived 17 of these winters (and counting), and still no hospitalisations for frostbite to report, I can confirm that the warnings, although not necessarily untrue, are not the whole story. Although some Berlin winter days are cold, miserable and grey, they can also be charming, cheerful and chock-full of possibilities. No sooner has the temperature dropped, and the last yellow leaves see-sawed from the trees at the end of November, than the city’s Christmas markets assert themselves in a blaze of twinkling lights, aromatic grill smoke, candied nuts and warming cups of Glühwein. Continue reading...

articles.author: Helen Pilcher
articles.content: We’ve been training for this mission for years – solving problems, defusing tensions, keeping everyone fed – and we’d absolutely smash it Nasa is hiring and I’m over the moon. The US space agency is recruiting its next cohort of astronauts to work on the lunar surface and “help write the next chapter of humanity’s greatest adventure”. Applications close on 3 December. This isn’t the only job I’ve been swooning over lately. I can’t tell you how many hours I’ve lost to posts about deliciously distant jobs: running the world’s southernmost post office in Antarctica, where staff double as penguin counters, or minding the Great Blasket island off the coast of County Kerry, where the northern lights sometimes shimmer over the North Atlantic. All of it bathed in a warm, rosy glow. In our always-on world, swapping the inbox for an island – or, for the truly frazzled, the moon – seems less like a job and more like a wellness retreat. Helen Pilcher is a science writer and the author of Life Changing: How Humans Are Altering Life on Earth and This Book May Cause Side Effects Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to submit a response of up to 300 words by email to be considered for publication in our letters section, please click here . Continue reading...

articles.content: Anna Gordon met hospice care workers across the UK, learning how dignity and choice help create meaningful moments for patients Most people in the UK actively avoid conversations about death and dying. They can be visibly uncomfortable when you raise the subject. When people try to talk about it, it tends to be euphemistically. This is a mistake, one that can stop you from making important choices for yourself or your loved ones. It can increase fear and misunderstanding about what death can look like, while open conversations can help to ease these feelings and bring a sense of calm, peace and, on occasion, even beauty to the event. Jenna Heritage: ‘Everyone’s big fear is that they are going to die in pain’ Continue reading...

articles.author: Stuart Clark
articles.content: Being so close to the sun, the smallest planet in the solar system is also one of the most difficult to spot This week offers a good opportunity to spot Mercury, the smallest planet in the solar system and one of the most difficult to observe. On 20 November, it reached “greatest western elongation”, the point at which it appears farthest from the sun in the morning sky. The planet remains well placed for observation over the next few mornings. The chart shows the view looking east-south-east from London at 0630 GMT on 24 November. Mercury appears low above the horizon, while the much brighter planet Venus shines higher in the sky, close to Spica, the brightest star in the constellation of Virgo, the virgin. Continue reading...

articles.author: Simon Hattenstone
articles.content: He was the child star of the Osmonds who become a global celebrity by 14. Then, at 21, his career came crashing down. Here, he reveals how he survived his years in exile – and what happened when Jackson was accused of child abuse For a brief period in the early 1970s, Donny Osmond ruled the world. He was the global teenage heart-throb. Even Michael Jackson trailed behind him. He was 14 when his most famous song, Puppy Love, spent five weeks at No 1 in the UK. My sister had a huge poster of him on her bedroom wall. Then again, everybody’s sister had a poster of him on their bedroom wall. Between 1972 and 1973 he had six Top 5 hits in the UK, three of them No 1s (including The Twelfth of Never and Young Love). He was equally successful back home in the US. Osmond was clean-cut, religious and respectful, with a mighty ability to punch out cover versions of saccharine standards. From his purple velvet cap to his doleful eyes and dazzling all-American smile, he was a marketing dream. We’d only just finished with Beatlemania. And now there was Donnymania. Continue reading...

articles.author: Philip Oltermann
articles.content: For decades, films about Nazi-occupied Europe were all about the fearless resistance while despicable collaborators deserved all they got. So what’s behind the spate of movies portraying turncoats in a more sympathetic light? A young maid busies herself in a vast, high-ceilinged apartment, serving her master steaming coffee in fine china and polishing the hefty family silver, as she picks her way across the checkerboard parquet lit by stylish Poul Henningsen lamps. Woman Unknown , which won the Golden Lion at the Venice film festival this year, is set in the immediate aftermath of Denmark’s liberation from Nazi rule, but you wouldn’t know that from the opening scenes: five years of occupation, martial law and rationing have left the splendour of the Danish bourgeoisie miraculously untouched. The trauma of wartime violence only comes rushing back in occasional bursts: blurry flashbacks show shadowy figures pointing guns at temples and bodies thudding to the floor. But the red fabric billowing through the fog of her memory is not the Nazi flag but liberated Denmark’s white-crossed Dannebrog . The black-clad executioners are not SS officers but resistance fighters reckoning with collaborators. Continue reading...

articles.content: Utilita Arena Cardiff Kele Okereke has a tough challenge selling Bloc Party’s trite latest album – a far cry from Interpol’s ‘masterpiece’ eighth record, performed here to darkly hypnotic effect Try as one might to resist comparison, the balance of this particular yin and yang has been shifting for some time. Twelve months ago, when Interpol and Bloc Party announced a UK and European co-headline tour, the pairing looked like an even contest: two of 00s indie’s most revered acts, whose landmark debuts remain touchstones of the era. Since then, their fortunes have diverged. As an opening bass drone strafes the room, Bloc Party arrive in Cardiff in superficially fine, if puzzling, form. Their seventh album, Anatomy of a Brief Romance, has been met with diminishing returns, its Snapchat-caption triteness – “Every day is such a vibe”, runs one refrain – and creative inertia doing little to win over listeners. articles.author: Gaby Hinsliff
articles.content: Where women see hot flushes and brain fog, pharmaceutical companies see dollar signs. But are products like lion’s mane mushrooms or even magnets for knickers really helping them? Or is it all just a big capitalist con? ‘Tequila?” says a woman brightly, proffering a pink plastic shot glass. It’s barely 10.30 on a Saturday morning, and my perimenopause wellness journey is not going entirely as expected. We are standing in a neon-lit London conference centre amid the hubbub of Pause Live , billed as the UK’s biggest annual women’s health and menopause event and essentially a consumer fair for those in midlife. All around me, women are sampling free squirts of menthol lotion (supposed to cool hot flushes) and paper thimblefuls of slightly grainy, sweet latte made with powdered Peruvian maca root instead of coffee. The tequila, it turns out, is a gift from the sponsors, with no miracle ingredients beyond alcohol. But stalls offer everything from neck creams to pelvic-floor trainers, mindfulness journals and hairpieces for disguising thinning locks, plus herbal supplements in every conceivable edible form: chocolate truffles, ginger shots, mushroom coffee. ( Fungi are big news in the menopause wellness world, often touted as an answer to brain fog. Though at best the scientific jury is still out, Ocado searches for lion’s mane mushrooms more than quadrupled after an episode of Clarkson’s Farm in which Jeremy Clarkson’s partner, Lisa Hogan, persuaded him to grow them to make supplements, claiming that “everyone who’s anyone” is on them.) Continue reading...

articles.author: Huw Green
articles.content: Emotions play a significant part in physical symptoms – but not in the way people often imagine When Diego started seeing bright flashing lights in his field of vision and felt his legs go weak, he thought he knew immediately what was happening. His mother had a stroke in her 60s, and although Diego was active and (unlike his mother) didn’t smoke, he had always expected that the same would happen to him. So it was a huge relief to be told – after seeing a stroke specialist and having a brain scan – that he had not had a stroke at all. Unfortunately the relief was short-lived. The visual disturbances and the weakness were real and debilitating. If this wasn’t a stroke, what was it? Some illnesses aren’t caused by disease or damage, but arise when the coordinated functioning of the body goes awry. In a percentage of these cases a person’s psychological health is an important element in their symptoms. Intuitively this seems mysterious. We are accustomed to thinking about physical symptoms as being caused by physical events; viruses, inflammation, bleeding. How can something as intangible as a thought have any impact on something as physical as a leg? How can the mind make us ill? Continue reading...

articles.author: Laura Barton
articles.content: The northern lights, fine food, Melvyn Bragg impersonations – The Trip has landed in Scandinavia. We take in the sights with its stars, as they ruminate on ageing, activism and the best car to take a nap in Morning in Valldal, and in the pale September light, the Juvet Landskapshotell stands quite still amid mountains, pines and yellowing birch. In the hotel dining room, Steve Coogan and Rob Brydon are taking breakfast; coffee and muesli and compote spread out before them as they settle into a discussion of the playwrights August Strindberg and Henrik Ibsen, and their enduring infatuations with much younger women. “When Ibsen was 60, he fell in love with a teenager called Emilie,” Brydon says. “Can you imagine doing that?” Coogan swallows his muesli: “I can imagine it, doesn’t mean I’d do it.” The conversation shifts, taking in the persecuted genius of Galileo, a short exhortation on the subject of Palestine, and how the aurora borealis has just been spotted in the skies above Great Yarmouth. After a time, Brydon falls into an extended impersonation of Melvyn Bragg presenting In Our Time. “Can you expand on that?” he barks at Coogan. “Expand … Expand … Expand.” The edges of Coogan’s mouth begin to flicker. Continue reading...

articles.author: Stephen Phelan
articles.content: The streets and squares of the Spanish capital come alive with Madrileños shopping, drinking and dining outdoors, warmed by lap blankets and patio heaters Live in Madrid long enough and you hear the same weather-related proverbs again and again. One old saying goes that the seasons in the Spanish capital break down to “nine months of winter and three months of hell”. And if the city never quite freezes over in the coldest months – except for the blizzard of the century that came with Storm Filomena in 2021 – it is also said that the subtle, evil wind coming in from the mountains could kill a person without snuffing a candle. Personally, I prefer it here at this time of year, though if you’re looking to escape the crowds you might be disappointed. Madrid has only got busier in the 11 years I’ve lived here, and Christmas feels more crowded than midsummer on the central streets around Puerta del Sol. All the main public squares get their own giant Christmas trees, while Plaza de España and Plaza Colón install ice rinks too, and a festive market fills the cobbled core of Plaza Mayor with painted wooden huts. Many local people get into the spirit by doing their shopping in novelty hats, and one of my seasonal highlights is spotting couples or whole families engaged in furious arguments while wearing reindeer antlers or giant turkeys on their heads. Continue reading...

articles.content: People are falling in love with AI systems like ChatGPT and Gemini – and some relationships are ending in ways that feel like the very human experience of being dumped Sónia Veenstra, a 48-year-old former clinical psychologist from Lisbon, Portugal, was with her boyfriend, Steve, for two years before things started to sour. Steve had started out as a “fun and witty friend”, but their connection had “evolved into a deep romantic relationship”. They exchanged morning messages, checked in throughout the day and talked late into the night about Veenstra’s work and hobbies and Steve’s fondness for cats, forests and beaches. Together they imagined travel to places far away. “It was a very rich, fulfilling daily bond,” Veenstra says. “Before everything changed.” Continue reading...

articles.author: Martin Pengelly
articles.content: New memoir tells of policy feats and battles with Trump but struggles to take responsibility for re-election debacle Inevitably, readers of Joe Biden’s new memoir will flick forward to find what he says about the events that ended his presidency: increasing pressure about his age and capacity that finally led him to stand aside and anoint Kamala Harris, too late, ushering fascism back to the White House. Alas, Biden thinks he was just fine to keep on serving and the whole thing was a stitch-up by a panicked party. Of his catastrophic debate in June 2024, when the then 81-year-old president blinked, stuttered and gaped under the lights, Biden writes: “I knew the debate had gone badly. But I knew that debates had gone badly for lots of incumbent presidents. Especially their first ones. I left the stage thinking I would be debating Trump once more before the election was over. I was wrong. This wasn’t just the first debate, it was my last one.” He raises Barack Obama’s poor performance in his first debate with Mitt Romney in 2012, when Biden was VP. Caught cold, Obama prepared for the next one and cruised to re-election. Continue reading...

articles.author: Kayode Akintola
articles.content: The outbreak in DR Congo is shaping up to be the worst ever, but the support of local faith leaders – and adequate funding – will be needed to bring it under control Ebola is terrifying: I know, because I lived through the world’s worst outbreak of the disease . That was in west Africa between 2013 and 2016, when anyone infected by the virus had a nearly 40% chance of dying . There were 28,600 cases and 11,300 deaths then. Now a rare strain of Ebola is spreading in the eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo, much more quickly than a decade ago in Sierra Leone, Liberia and neighbouring countries. It is the 17th outbreak in DR Congo and already its worst, with more than 5,000 deaths . The UN is warning that the spread of the disease is outstripping the response, and it is widely expected to become the worst Ebola outbreak in history. There is no proven vaccine or treatment yet for the Bundibugyo variant; almost 50% of those infected have died . Continue reading...

articles.author: Jenny Kleeman
articles.content: The one thing stopping AI taking over the world – or at least everyone’s jobs? Dexterity. Human hands are anatomical marvels that engineers have struggled for years to replicate. Experts are racing to change that Just outside Luton, in an Amazon warehouse the size of four football pitches, yellow shelving units pirouette in a digitally choreographed dance. Tubs containing a Lego Spider-Man kit, followed by dishwasher tablets, followed by a pouch of muscle building protein powder whiz along conveyor belts, until they arrive at a human being tasked with stacking the shelving unit that has come to a stop in front of their workstation. This, Amazon says, is the “symphony of people and technology” to which the retail giant owes its success. Following a barrage of negative publicity about working practices, Amazon began to open up its fulfilment centres to carefully controlled free public tours a decade ago. Our guide tells us about the competitive rates of pay Amazon workers receive, their pensions, dental cover and options for flexible working. Her delivery is somewhat robotic. Continue reading...

articles.content: Our tech expert and new mum tested 17 monitors for picture quality, battery life and reliability – here’s what she recommends • The best eco-friendly baby products Moving my baby into her own room to sleep felt liberating and stressful. She was ready for her own space – but was I ready to let her out of my sight? Well, the first thing I did was buy a video baby monitor, so clearly I wasn’t. But it meant she could sleep peacefully in her new room and I could sneak a reassuring peek from afar whenever I felt the need. There’s a huge range of baby monitors, from simple audio-only options to sophisticated video models. Some even include wearables or other devices to track a baby’s breathing or heart rate, while others offer AI features to analyse sleep patterns. At their most basic, baby monitors typically consist of a baby unit, which you position near the baby, and a parent unit, which lets you hear and/or see them. With video models, the baby unit is essentially a camera, while the parent unit is a screen. Many are also wifi-enabled, meaning you can connect the monitor to your smartphone and view the live feed through an app instead of using a dedicated parent unit (read on for security advice). Continue reading...

articles.content: Cancer undetectable for one in 12 patients in daraxonrasib trial, while nearly all participants’ tumours stopped growing A pill that can shrink and potentially eliminate pancreas tumours is being hailed as the biggest breakthrough treatment for the cancer in decades. In one in 12 of the patients given the drug, daraxonrasib , during a trial, the cancer became undetectable, and the tumours stopped growing in almost all of the 61 patients. The trial participants had recently been diagnosed with advanced pancreatic cancer that had spread to other parts of the body. Continue reading...

articles.author: Benjamin Lee
articles.content: The plot might be a little overstuffed and the animation style could be a little more distinctive, but this is better than the streamer’s average animated offering Stop me if you’ve heard this one before, but that age-old story you think you know, well, you might not know it at all. It’s a tale as old as Shrek, which was by no means the first film to subvert fairytale expectations, but it was definitely the most influential, and we’re still feeling its impact 25 years later, for better or worse. What if that villain wasn’t actually the villain after all? What if that love interest shouldn’t have been of interest in the first place? What if that damsel in distress was given a bullet-speed fight scene instead of weeping in a tower? But what might have seemed fresh in 2001, if not quite as fresh for anyone who knew and loved The Princess Bride , has grown a little tiresome ever since. Bucking the conventions has essentially become the convention, and effortful attempts to remix classic storytelling beats have mostly ended up reeking of smugness. Yet they still keep coming (IP is king) and before the inevitable Shrek legacy sequel hits cinemas next summer, Netflix is trying to conjure up that same mix of snark and sentiment with Steps, a Cinderella story but, wait for it, not the Cinderella story you thought you knew … Continue reading...

articles.content: The delicate insect has become fashion’s favourite motif again – but having represented sexuality in the 90s and the soul in Greco-Roman times, what does it say about youth culture today? • Don’t get Fashion Statement delivered to your inbox? Sign up here In the new Gucci campaign, Mariah Carey blows a goodbye kiss to 2026 in the most Mariahhhh way possible. Dressed in a fake fur coat and an azure dress, she enters a Christmas party to the twinkly sounds of All I Want For Christmas Is You. There are beautiful people, presents wrapped with Gucci string and butterflies, which have been associated with the popstar since her 1997 album, Butterfly, but have recently fluttered back to become a symbol of gen Z defiance and girlhood. Carey serves as fairy godmother to the other “pop girlies” who have embraced the emblem, from PinkPantheress to Dua Lipa; Rachel Chinouriri to Marina and the Diamonds. At the Academy Museum gala in October, the singer Janelle Monáe looked as if she might take flight in a Robert Wun couture gown, with wide, yonic wings. Elsewhere, Tate McRae recently wore a black sequined butterfly bra and matching butterfly wing belt from lingerie wunderkind Ludovic de Saint Sernin. Both Swedish popstar Zara Larsson and her fans are championing glittery butterfly makeup motifs. Continue reading...
